object: a stout deerstalker detective pig, an oversized magnifying glass, and a curious toy aunt hen
morph: playful stroke pieces dodge the pig's magnifier from the edges until 姑 forms

promptEn: An 8-second silly animated clip, bright pastel look, soft daylight, no dark grading. In a chocolate-brown and cream toy study with a green desk lamp, a stout detective pig in a checked cap lugs a magnifying glass nearly as big as himself. 0–1.7s: The first 姑 is spoken as a coral 女 stroke peeks in from the left edge, then ducks away as the pig swings his magnifier, whacking the lamp. 1.7–3.3s: The second 姑 is spoken: a 古 piece pokes from the top, dodges, scoots under the desk, and the pig dives after it with his magnifier lens stuck on his snout. 3.3–4.9s: Both pieces tiptoe out together; the pig freezes, they freeze, then he sneezes and they hop into place, making 姑 in warm terracotta. 4.9–5.9s: As 姑丈 is spoken, a dapper toy beaver in a bow tie peeks from behind the lamp and tips a hat; the pig does a startled double-take. Final hold (about 5.0–8.0s): the pig polishes his lens beaming while the beaver winks; the glyph is completely still. Audio: a warm off-screen voice in clear Taiwanese Mandarin reads exactly this line, slowly and distinctly with the marked tones, then stops: 姑、姑、姑丈（ㄍㄨ、ㄍㄨ、ㄍㄨ ㄓㄤˋ）. The first 姑 lands at about 0.9s, the second 姑 at about 2.6s, and the word 姑丈 at about 5.0s, each timed to the picture described above. On-screen text is limited to the one glyph 姑 in strong solid color over a light bright background; the spoken word is never shown as text. The glyph 姑 fills roughly 70% of frame height, centered and uncropped, and stays perfectly still for the final 3 seconds while the lead keeps playing away from the strokes. No real people, no flashing.

object: a chunky toy warrior with a foam sword and round shield, facing a sky-high wobbling stack of eight terracotta foam swords carried by Peanut the raccoon, with a small round hatbox balanced on top
morph: the warrior's huge swing whiffs and spins him around; one tiny poke tips the towering stack over like a falling tree, and the eight bouncing foam swords land as the eight strokes of 姑 — three bending into 女 on the left, five straight ones stacking into 古 on the right
creativeAngle: 全新「以小搏大」肢體笑料：小小玩具戰士面對浣熊花生扛著的摩天泡棉劍塔（八支劍＝八個筆畫），先是用力過猛轉圈撲空，再輕輕一戳讓整座塔像大樹一樣「咚」地倒下，泡棉劍彈落排成「姑」。說「姑姑」時帽盒彈開、木頭姑姑小玩偶揮手，聲音與畫面同步。和前版豬探長的躲貓貓完全不同，改為四段清楚升級的動作節奏。
promptEn: An 8-second slapstick animated clip, bright pastel look, soft even daylight, no dark grading. Setting: a plain cream playroom floor with a pale peach wall, nothing busy behind. Lead: a chunky toy warrior, small and squat, with a floppy foam sword, a round red shield and a huge confident grin, all bravado and no skill. Rival: Peanut, a cartoon raccoon sidekick, almost hidden under a wobbling tower of eight terracotta-red foam swords stacked far too tall, with a small round hatbox balanced on the very top. 0–1.5s: the tiny warrior stands at lower left, plants his feet and points his sword up as the giant sword-tower stomps in from the right, swaying over him like a bragging giant; Peanut salutes at the wrong moment, letting go with one paw so the tower lurches even taller. The first 姑 is spoken at about 0.8s as the tower first looms over him. 1.5–3.2s: the warrior winds up with a big heroic swing, misses the tower completely, and the force spins him around twice on one foot until he plops down dizzy on his bottom with crossed eyes; the tower keeps blustering forward, leaning down over him. 3.2–4.9s: a frozen half-second of anticipation, then the warrior simply reaches up and gives the bottom sword one tiny poke with his fingertip. The whole tower tips sideways like a falling tree and lands across the frame with a soft cartoon THUMP and a dust puff; the eight foam swords bounce once and settle as the eight strokes of the glyph 姑 in saturated terracotta red: on the left three swords bend into the slanted and curving strokes of 女, and on the right five straight swords stack into 古 with 十 above a neat square 口. The second 姑 is spoken at about 4.2s as the strokes snap into place. 4.9–5.6s: Peanut lies flat on his back in the lower-left corner, grinning and saluting; the warrior climbs onto his belly and strikes a victory pose. The word 姑姑 is spoken at about 5.0s exactly as the little hatbox in the lower-right corner pops its lid and a wooden peg-doll auntie figurine with a hair bun and polka-dot apron springs up on a coil and waves cheerfully. Final hold (5.0–8.0s): the finished glyph 姑 stays perfectly still, centered and uncropped, filling about 70% of frame height with clear margins, while away from the strokes the warrior raises his sword, spins himself around again, wobbles and grins, Peanut salutes from the floor, and the peg-doll auntie keeps waving. Audio: a warm, friendly off-screen voice in clear Taiwanese Mandarin reads exactly these syllables, slowly and distinctly with clear tones, then stops: 姑、姑、姑姑（ㄍㄨ、ㄍㄨ、ㄍㄨ ㄍㄨ）. No other dialogue, no music louder than the voice, no loud startling sounds. On-screen text is limited to the single glyph 姑 in solid terracotta red over the light cream background; the spoken word is never shown as text, no subtitles, no watermark, no flashing. Cartoon bonks only, nobody hurt; all characters are clearly toys and cartoon animals, no real people.

conceptZh: 發條鯊魚踮腳偷溜去咬姑姑造型餅乾罐裡的長棍餅乾，卻一口咬錯咬到打瞌睡的拉布拉多警長的哨子，嗶一聲兩人面對面尖叫，警長衝過頭撞翻罐子，八根餅乾飛散落地拼成「姑」。
object: a chunky teal wind-up toy shark with a big brass key on its back, and a big friendly cartoon Labrador sheriff dog with a star badge and a whistle, dozing beside a plump ceramic cookie jar shaped like a smiling auntie in a flowered hat, filled with eight long breadstick biscuits
morph: the sheriff skids past the spinning shark and bonks the auntie cookie jar; eight breadstick biscuits fly out and clatter down as the eight strokes of 姑 — three bending into 女 on the left, five forming 十 over a square 口 on the right — while the jar rolls to the corner and its hat-lid pops up to wave
creativeAngle: The earlier versions used a pig detective and a toy warrior, and each one tacked a separate auntie figure on at the end. This time the auntie is the thing being guarded. The cookie jar is shaped like a smiling auntie, so 姑姑 is in the picture from the very first frame and wakes up and waves when the word is spoken. The shark's habit of biting the wrong thing drives the gag: it chomps the whistle, which wakes the sheriff. The strokes come from eight breadsticks that the crash scatters onto the floor, and the 女 and 古 halves are spelled out so the structure stays correct.
promptEn:
An 8-second slapstick cartoon, bright pastel look, soft even daylight, plain cream floor and pale mint wall, nothing busy behind. Lead: a chunky teal wind-up toy shark with a brass key turning on its back, stubby clockwork feet and a huge toothy grin, greedy and clumsy. Guard: a big friendly cartoon Labrador sheriff dog with a gold star badge and a silver whistle on a cord, snoozing sitting up on the right beside a plump ceramic cookie jar shaped like a smiling auntie in a flowered hat, with eight long breadstick biscuits sticking out of its top.
0–1.8s: The shark peeks in from the left, sees the breadsticks, drools and licks its lips. As it lifts one foot high to start tiptoeing, the first 姑 is spoken at about 0.9s.
1.8–3.4s: Huge exaggerated high steps, each one going SQUEAK. The shark freezes each time while the sheriff snores and his whistle bobs. It reaches the jar, opens wide, chomps... and bites the sheriff's whistle by mistake. TWEEEET! The sheriff's eyes snap open, and nose to nose they both scream with mouths huge and ears flapping.
3.4–5.0s: The shark spins in frantic circles on dry land, key whirring. The sheriff charges to stop it, skids right past it on his paws and BONKS into the cookie jar. The jar tips, and the eight breadsticks fly up and clatter down at center as the glyph 姑 in saturated terracotta red: on the left, three sticks bend into the strokes of 女; on the right, five sticks form 十 over a neat square 口. The second 姑 is spoken at about 4.6s as the last stick snaps into place. The jar rolls to the lower-right corner.
5.0s: The word 姑姑 is spoken as the auntie jar sits upright in the corner, pops up its flowered hat-lid like a greeting, and waves one little ceramic hand with a warm smile.
Final hold 5.0–8.0s: The glyph 姑 stays perfectly still, centered and uncropped, filling about 70% of frame height with clear margins. Away from the strokes, the sheriff sits dazed in the lower left with a dizzy grin and twirling stars, the shark wobbles to a stop and does a tiny happy wiggle, and the auntie jar keeps waving.
Audio: a warm, friendly off-screen voice in clear Taiwanese Mandarin reads exactly these syllables, slowly and distinctly with clear tones, then stops: 姑、姑、姑姑（ㄍㄨ、ㄍㄨ、ㄍㄨ ㄍㄨ）. Squeaks, the tweet and the soft bonk are gentle, and there is no other dialogue and no music louder than the voice. The only on-screen text is the single glyph 姑 on the light background: no subtitles, no watermark, no flashing. Cartoon bonks only, nobody hurt. All characters are clearly toys and cartoon animals.
